reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: The biliary manifestation of systemic IgG4-related disease, and the most common extra-pancreatic organ involvement in type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis
Usually presents with obstructive jaundice, most often from a stricture of the distal bile duct, closely mimicking pancreatic or biliary malignancy
Can also produce proximal, hilar, or intrahepatic strictures that resemble primary sclerosing cholangitis or cholangiocarcinoma
Raised serum IgG4 supports the diagnosis, but is neither wholly sensitive nor specific and can be mildly elevated in cholangiocarcinoma and PSC
Bile duct wall biopsy or ampullary biopsy showing dense IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis is confirmatory
The hallmark is a striking response to corticosteroids, with resolution of strictures and jaundice, unlike primary sclerosing cholangitis
Management is corticosteroid induction with biliary stenting as needed for obstruction, and immunomodulators or rituximab for relapsing disease
reference.pathophysiology: IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis is part of the systemic fibroinflammatory spectrum of IgG4-related disease. An aberrant immune response leads to infiltration of the bile duct walls by IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes, accompanied by storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. This transmural inflammation thickens the duct wall and narrows the lumen, producing single or multiple strictures anywhere along the biliary tree, though the intrapancreatic distal bile duct is most often affected, frequently in association with autoimmune pancreatitis. Because the process is immune-mediated rather than fixed fibrotic scarring, it characteristically regresses with immunosuppression, distinguishing it from primary sclerosing cholangitis.
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma with biliary obstruction
additionalInvestigations: MRI with MRCP to map the strictures and assess the pancreas and other organs
Serum IgG4 and total IgG with subclass analysis
Endoscopic ultrasound or cholangioscopy with biopsy to exclude cholangiocarcinoma
Ampullary or bile duct biopsy for IgG4 immunostaining and characteristic histology
Assessment for other IgG4-related organ involvement (pancreas, salivary glands, kidneys, retroperitoneum)
Serum CA 19-9 to help weigh malignancy
Documentation of biochemical and radiological response to a corticosteroid trial
redFlags: A dominant or mass-forming stricture with features suspicious for cholangiocarcinoma
Markedly raised CA 19-9 or progressive weight loss
Failure of jaundice or strictures to respond to corticosteroids
Progression to biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension
reference.prognosis: The condition typically responds rapidly and completely to corticosteroids with resolution of strictures and jaundice; relapse is common in systemic IgG4-related disease and may require maintenance therapy, and untreated or refractory disease can progress to secondary biliary cirrhosis.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the disease as primary sclerosing cholangitis and missing its steroid responsiveness
Overlooking cholangiocarcinoma, which can coexist with or mimic the condition and may itself raise IgG4
Relying on serum IgG4 alone for diagnosis given its imperfect specificity
Committing to major biliary surgery for a presumed malignant stricture that is in fact steroid-responsive disease
Failing to look for associated autoimmune pancreatitis and other organ involvement
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
HISORt and international criteria for IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
Reviews of IgG4-related disease and cholangiopathy
management: Exclude cholangiocarcinoma with imaging and biopsy before treating, as the presentation closely mimics biliary malignancy
Induce remission with corticosteroids, expecting striking resolution of strictures and jaundice
Add azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab for maintenance or relapsing disease
Relieve significant biliary obstruction or cholangitis with endoscopic stenting
Treat coexisting type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis as part of the same disease process
Monitor liver function, serum IgG4 and MRCP for relapse and progression towards secondary biliary cirrhosis
Manage through hepatobiliary and pancreatology services
